title: Research Bite #37: Prior knowledge activation as preparation prior to instruction
author: Craig Barton
summary: Research Bite #37 summarizes Charleen Brand, Katharina Loibl, and Nikol Rummel's study of how activating prior knowledge before instruction supports learning inside two-phase instructional designs like Productive Failure and Vicarious Failure. Working with 165 secondary students, the researchers manipulated how much of a target concept's conceptual components were represented in the preparatory solution attempts students studied, comparing high-coverage and low-coverage conditions. The key finding challenges an intuitive assumption: activating only some relevant prior knowledge was sufficient to prepare students for the subsequent explicit instruction, and this held true across all levels of students' initial prior knowledge, not just for already-strong students. The researchers also identify 'intermediate knowledge' — the knowledge state formed during the preparatory phase — as the mechanism linking prior-knowledge activation to eventual conceptual learning, with the follow-up explicit instruction acting as a kind of delayed feedback that helps students reconcile what they activated with the canonical solution. For teachers using preparatory or failure-based activities before direct instruction, the practical message is to aim for 'enough' relevant activation rather than exhaustive coverage of every component of a new concept.
points: Activating some relevant prior knowledge before instruction was sufficient to prepare students for learning — comprehensive coverage of every conceptual component was not necessary.

The benefit held across all levels of prior knowledge, not just for high-attaining students, countering the idea that preparatory activities like Productive Failure only help students who already know a lot.

“Intermediate knowledge” — what students construct during the preparatory phase — is the proposed mechanism linking prior-knowledge activation to later conceptual learning, with explicit instruction functioning as delayed feedback that helps consolidate it.

The study's dependent variable had a skewed distribution and a narrow definition of “relevant prior knowledge,” so teachers should treat the specific coverage threshold as provisional rather than a precise recipe.
quotes: This research investigates how activating prior knowledge prepares secondary school students for learning new concepts within two-phase instructional designs like Productive Failure (PF) and Vicarious Failure (VF).

the findings suggest that activating some relevant knowledge is sufficient for preparation, even if it doesn't encompass all aspects of the target concept, benefiting students across all levels of initial prior knowledge.
Activating some relevant prior knowledge before instruction is beneficial for students of all levels of prior knowledge.
This paper provides first causal empirical evidence on the conditions under which intermediate knowledge facilitates students' learning from instruction.
Activating some relevant knowledge can prepare students for subsequent instruction and benefit students of all levels of prior knowledge
the experimental conditions' differences might have been too small, as both included crucial prerequisite components, possibly yielding similar outcomes.
